metadata.title: Hardening Staging — Revision Tracking, Logging & Monitoring
metadata.source: Fellow-supplied 7-slide narration script (post-deploy smoke testing, Cloud Run revisions, traffic management, centralized logging, monitoring/alerting), provided 2026-10-08. Continues medas-stage-environment-provisioning, medas-stage-environment-security and medas-stage-pipeline-validation.
metadata.description: Hardening the staging environment from merely functional into observable and self-verifying: an automated post-deploy smoke test gate, Cloud Run's immutable-revision model and what it enables, traffic splitting/pinning across revisions, centralized structured logging via Cloud Logging, and basic monitoring/alerting on latency, error rate and traffic volume -- closing on staging now meeting the same bar production will need to meet.
metadata.note: GitHub-dark skin for the five mechanics beats (GitHubCallChain diagrams, matching the supplied slide structure), Claude-cream skin for the INTRO bookend, the outcome card, and the OUTRO. Narration text is the fellow-supplied script verbatim -- no garbling this time, no repairs needed.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude cream skin, slide 1 title card
beats.narration_text: With the staging pipeline fully functional, this week's focus shifted from just deploying successfully to deploying with confidence — adding the visibility and safety checks needed to treat staging like a real pre-production environment.

props.runningText: smoke test → immutable revisions → traffic control → logging → monitoring…
output: from deploying successfully to deploying with confidence

beats.role_note: slide 2 -- automated health check gate after every deploy
beats.narration_text: The pipeline now runs an automated smoke test immediately after every staging deployment — hitting the live service and confirming it responds correctly before the deployment is considered successful. This closes the gap between 'the deploy command finished' and 'the application is actually healthy,' catching issues the moment they happen instead of relying on someone noticing later.

nodes.d: hits the live service, confirms it responds correctly

props.caption: Closes the gap between 'the command finished' and 'the application is actually healthy.'

beats.narration_text: Every deployment to Cloud Run creates a new, immutable revision rather than overwriting the running one. The service's traffic is then simply pointed at the new revision. This matters because old revisions aren't discarded — they remain available, which is what makes both rollback and controlled traffic shifting possible without rebuilding anything.

nodes.d: creates a new, immutable revision — never overwrites the running one
service traffic now points at the new revision
not discarded — available for rollback or traffic shifting

props.caption: Rollback and traffic shifting both work because nothing was rebuilt or overwritten to get here.

beats.role_note: slide 4 -- split or pin traffic across revisions
beats.narration_text: Beyond simple all-or-nothing deploys, Cloud Run supports directing traffic across revisions — including pinning traffic back to a known-good revision instantly if needed. Building this awareness into the staging process now means the same traffic-control safety net is already understood and ready to extend into production.

nodes.d: e.g. 90/10 — a gradual rollout, not a switch flip

props.caption: Proven in staging now, so the same safety net is already understood before production needs it.

beats.role_note: slide 5 -- Cloud Logging, searchable structured logs
beats.narration_text: All application and request logs from the staging service now flow into Cloud Logging automatically, giving a centralized, searchable view of exactly what the service is doing — without needing to SSH into anything or dig through container output manually.

nodes.d: flows in automatically — no agent to configure
no SSH, no digging through container output

props.caption: Centralized by default — the logging pipeline isn't something that had to be separately built.

beats.narration_text: On top of logging, I set up basic monitoring for the staging service — tracking key signals like request latency, error rate, and traffic volume. This gives a real-time, at-a-glance view of service health, turning staging into an environment that doesn't just run the application, but actively tells you how well it's running.

nodes.d: built on top of the same logs and metrics

props.caption: Staging now tells you how well it's running, not just that it ran.

beats.role_note: slide 7 -- the verdict card, Claude cream skin
beats.narration_text: By the end of this week, staging isn't just a place deployments land — it's a self-verifying environment with automated health checks, revision-based safety, and real visibility into its own health. That's the same bar production will need to meet, and now it's already proven out here.
